title: Demonstrate knowledge of the factors that affect the exportation of perishable produce

lessons.title: Global factors and the need to comply
lessons.html:
Global factors that affect perishable exports

A South African fruit grower competes in a world market. What happens in other countries affects prices, demand and the rules for getting fruit in. The main global factors are:

  • Counter-seasonal supply: South Africa is in the Southern Hemisphere, so our fruit is harvested when Europe and North America are in winter or spring. This gives our exports a natural window, but other Southern Hemisphere suppliers such as Chile, Peru, Argentina, Australia and New Zealand compete in the same window.
  • World supply and demand: a big crop in a competing country lowers prices; a poor crop raises them.
  • Trade agreements: agreements between South Africa and trading partners, such as with the European Union, affect import duties and quotas.
  • Economic conditions: recessions, inflation and consumer spending power in importing countries affect demand for premium fruit.
  • Global events: pandemics, wars and shipping disruptions affect shipping routes, costs and demand.
  • Consumer trends: demand for healthy food, convenience packs, organic produce and sustainably and ethically produced fruit.

Why compliance with local and international requirements matters

Every importing country sets rules to protect its consumers and its own agriculture. South Africa also has its own export standards. Fruit that does not comply will be rejected, delayed or destroyed, at great cost.

  • Local requirements: export standards under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990, inspected by PPECB, and cold chain control under the PPECB Act 9 of 1983.
  • International requirements: phytosanitary rules against pests and diseases, maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides, food safety and labelling laws.
  • Private standards: retailer requirements such as GLOBALG.A.P. and ethical trade audits.

Non-compliance by one exporter can lead to stricter controls for all South African fruit. That is why compliance is not just a cost; it is how the whole industry keeps its market access.

lessons.title: Market forces and external factors
lessons.html:
Market forces

Market forces are the economic pressures that determine what is sold, where and at what price.

  • Supply and demand: when many cartons arrive in a market at once, prices drop. Exporters try to spread supply to avoid gluts.
  • Competition: other countries and other South African exporters compete for the same buyers and shelf space.
  • Buyer power: large supermarket chains set specifications, prices and programmes, and can switch suppliers.
  • Exchange rate: fruit is often sold in foreign currency such as euros, pounds or dollars. A weaker rand increases the rand value of each carton sold; a stronger rand reduces it.
  • Quality and reputation: consistent quality earns repeat business and better prices.
  • New markets: opening markets such as China, India or the Middle East spreads risk but each market has its own requirements.

External factors

External factors are outside the control of the farm or exporter but affect the potential to export:

  • Climate and weather: drought, hail, floods, heat waves and frost reduce volume and quality.
  • Water availability: water restrictions in dry years limit production.
  • Pests and diseases: outbreaks of fruit fly, false codling moth or new pests can close markets.
  • Infrastructure: port efficiency, road and rail condition, electricity supply for cold stores, and container availability.
  • Input costs: fuel, electricity, fertiliser, chemicals, packaging and labour.
  • Political and labour issues: strikes, policy changes and trade disputes.
  • Shipping costs and routes: freight rates and transit times.

Example: load-shedding at a packhouse means generators must run the cold rooms, raising costs. At the same time a port delay keeps containers waiting. The exporter must plan for these risks with back-up power, buffer time and good communication with the shipping line.

Key points

  • South Africa's counter-seasonal position gives a natural export window.
  • Compliance with local and international rules protects market access for everyone.
  • Supply, demand, competition and the exchange rate drive prices.
  • Weather, pests, infrastructure and input costs are key external factors.
  • Good planning reduces the impact of factors you cannot control.
